Binance Research on Key Trends in Crypto: October 2026

2026-10-14

Main Takeaways

  • This blog summarizes the findings of the recent Binance Research report discussing key developments of crypto markets in September 2026.

  • In September, total crypto market capitalization rose 11.0% to $2.99T, despite a challenging macro and policy backdrop.

  • Looking ahead, yields, Fed data, and CLARITY are key watchpoints.

Crypto markets rallied through a hawkish Fed and a stalled CLARITY Act in September, with spot ETF flows turning positive for the year and BTC notching its strongest September in four years. This blog breaks down Binance Research’s latest monthly report, covering crypto market performance, the major coins driving gains, and the key events to watch heading into October.

Crypto Market Performance in September 2026

In September, total crypto market capitalization rose 11.0% to $2.99T, despite a challenging macro and policy backdrop.

August inflation held at 3.4% and payrolls beat expectations. On September 16, the Fed raised rates 25 basis points to 3.75-4.00%, its first hike since July 2023, and 16 of 18 officials expect another by year-end.

The CLARITY Act stalled after a 49-50 cloture vote, though the CFTC and SEC moved crypto rules forward on September 18.

BTC still rallied. Spot ETFs drew $3.49B, turning 2026 flows positive, and Strategy bought 2,615 BTC. This made it the strongest of four straight positive Septembers.

Monthly crypto market capitalization grew 11.0% in September. Source: CoinGecko, Binance Research, as of September 30, 2026

Majors were broadly positive in September, with gains driven by ETF flows, institutional partnerships, and network catalysts.

ZEC led with 65.9%, reaching a market capitalization of roughly $24B as shielded pools neared record levels. LINK rose 26.7% after Circle launched Arc mainnet with Chainlink as its foundational oracle. SOL gained 19.1% as spot SOL ETFs posted their best week since launch and Solana stablecoins hit a record $17.3B. DOGE added 16.2% alongside the broader rally.

BNB rose 12.7%, and BNB Chain became the only chain holding $1B in tokenized stocks. ETH added 10.8% on $689.9M of weekly spot ETF inflows. HYPE was the weakest, up 4.3%, as its August rally cooled despite an all-time high on September 19.

Monthly price performance of the top 10 coins by market capitalization. Source: CoinGecko, Binance Research, as of September 30, 2026

October Watchpoints: Yields, Fed Data, and CLARITY

Rising Treasury yields remain the main risk to the crypto rally. The 10-year yield is at its highest since 2002, pushed up by energy-driven inflation risks, strong growth, and worries about government borrowing. 

As of late September, a softer-than-expected August PCE reading had cut the odds of an October Fed hike to about 35-40%, down from around 70% a week earlier, with September payrolls (released October 2) and CPI (due October 14) both key inputs ahead of the Fed’s late-October meeting. 

On the regulatory front, CLARITY can still return for another Senate vote, possibly after the November 3 midterms. In the meantime, comments on the SEC’s Regulation Crypto Assets proposal are due October 20.

Notable Events in October 2026

To help users stay on top of the latest Web3 news, the Binance Research team has summarized notable events and token unlocks across October, from scheduled unlocks to key dates in the regulatory calendar. Keep an eye on these developments as the month progresses, since any one of them could shift market sentiment.

Notable Events in October 2026. Source: Cryptoevents, Binance Research

Final Thoughts

This article is only a snapshot of the full report, which contains further analyses of the most important charts from the past month. The full report explores several themes shaping the market, including BTC’s strengthening trend reversal and growing sensitivity to real yields, a doubling in AI pre-IPO perpetuals volume as AI regulation and IPO timelines come into focus, and bStocks utilization of 11.2%, well ahead of the 7.4% industry level.

Binance Pay Expands Agentic Payments Into Real-World Commerce

2026-10-13

Main Takeaways

  • Binance Pay brings agentic payments into real-world commerce, letting AI agents and applications complete real transactions, starting with AI-powered hotel bookings.

  • It supports payments from self-custody wallets with no card details and no gas management, with settlement on BNB Chain.

  • Travelers can book from over 2.2 million accommodations via Travala’s AI travel agent, with up to 10% cashback in BNB and AVA on a first qualifying booking.

Until now, onchain payments have shared one assumption: a human is present at the moment of payment. AI agents can already search, compare, and find the right option, but they’ve always needed a human to open a wallet and confirm before anything can be paid for. 

Binance x402 closes that gap. You authorize the payment in advance, and your agent completes the transaction without needing you to confirm again in the moment. That’s the problem Binance Pay set out to solve with Binance x402, the payment infrastructure for agents, APIs, and digital services introduced earlier this year. Now, that work is reaching real-world commerce, starting with booking a hotel through an AI agent.

Bringing Agentic Payments to Hotel Bookings

Binance Pay has teamed up with BNB Chain and Travala to enable AI-powered hotel bookings using USDT on BNB Smart Chain. Travelers authorize payment from a self-custody wallet in advance, then search, choose, and book directly through Travala's AI travel agent, with Binance Pay handling execution and settlement: no card details, gas management, or currency conversion required. 

In this collaboration, BNB Chain provides the Machine Payments Protocol (MPP) SDK and agentic framework, and Binance Pay provides the payment settlement infrastructure. The launch is part of Binance Pay’s broader work on Agent Pay, which is building payment infrastructure for AI agents, applications and machine-driven commerce.

Get Up to 10% Back on Your First AI Agent Hotel Booking

Booking through an AI agent works a little differently from a standard checkout. You authorize payment in advance, so your agent can complete the booking without you confirming again at the moment of payment.

Authorize: Approve payment in advance using USDT from a BNB Smart Chain wallet.

Search: Tell Travala’s AI agent where and when you want to travel.

Choose: Select your preferred accommodation from Travala’s inventory presented by the AI agent.

Book: The agent completes payment and your booking is confirmed.

It all happens directly in the browser, with no set up required, no card information to enter, and no gas fees to manage. Hotel bookings are available at launch, with additional travel products expected to be supported in the future. 

To mark the launch, eligible travelers can receive 7% cashback in BNB on their first qualifying hotel booking through Travala’s AI travel agent. Eligible AVA Smart members can receive an additional 3% cashback in AVA. The promotion applies to qualifying bookings of at least US$400, subject to applicable eligibility requirements and promotion terms.

How Binance Pay Powers the Settlement

The biggest change with agent payments isn’t simply paying with crypto. It’s who has to manage the payment process.

User tells the agent what they want

The user chooses and authorizes. The agent and Binance Pay handle execution, settlement and confirmation behind the scenes. Here’s what that looks like technically. 

When a traveler confirms a booking, they sign an EIP-712 Permit2 authorization offchain. The MPP SDK verifies the signature, wallet balance, allowance, and payment parameters, then sends the verified payment instruction to Binance Pay. 

Binance Pay then broadcasts the transaction and pays the required network gas. Funds move from the user's wallet to Travala. Once settlement is complete, MPP marks the payment as successful and issues an onchain receipt confirming the transaction.

Building Payments for the Agent Economy

The Travala launch is one example of a broader shift in how payments may work as AI agents become more capable. Binance Pay is building toward a world where payments can become a native capability for AI applications, connecting agents with APIs, digital services, merchants and real-world commerce. 

Different use cases may rely on different protocols and agent frameworks, but the underlying requirement remains the same: AI agents need a reliable way to turn an authorized action into a completed payment. Binance Pay aims to provide that payment layer.

Final Thoughts: Toward Agent-Powered Commerce

Binance Pay is the payment service within the Binance ecosystem that enables eligible users to make and receive payments through supported payment experiences, with user-verification, risk-management, transaction-monitoring, and account-security controls built in. Agent Pay extends that same infrastructure to AI agents acting on a user’s behalf.

This is the shift Binance Pay is enabling: from users managing crypto transactions themselves to AI agents using crypto as a seamless payment rail to complete real tasks. The Travala hotel booking is the first example, with more travel products and use cases to follow. 

If you're building AI-agent platforms, APIs, or digital services, you can explore Binance Agent Pay and apply to integrate agentic payment capabilities into your own products.

The Active Strategy Gap: How Binance Capital Connect Links Capital With Performance

2026-10-13

Main Takeaways

  • Institutional capital is pouring into digital assets, with 86% of institutional investors holding or planning allocations in 2025, but almost all of it goes into passive products.

  • The gap isn’t unique to crypto. Capital raising everywhere favors size over performance, but crypto has no standardized way to discover or compare active managers at all.

  • Capital Connect closes that gap: an exchange-native marketplace to browse, evaluate, and allocate to active strategies, with verified data and zero platform fee.

Note: This is a general announcement. Certain products and services may not be available in your region. Terms and conditions apply. 

By 2025, 86% of institutional investors held or developed plans to allocate to digital assets, and 83% had committed to increasing their holdings, according to the EY-Parthenon 2025 Institutional Investor Digital Assets Survey. Capital is flowing in.

But almost all of it is going into passive products. The same EY survey found that 81% of institutional investors prefer spot exposure through a registered vehicle like an ETF. That solves for passive and beta exposure, but there is no equivalent on-ramp for active crypto portfolio managers. Dedicated crypto hedge fund AUM is only $10 to $15 billion despite the broader institutional wave, according to the Crypto Insights Group's 2025 Industry Guide.

Two-thirds of institutional investors allocate to digital assets, but over one-third keep exposure below 2%, and 41% said they would increase exposure if operational and compliance risks were reduced, as per the 7th Annual Global Crypto Hedge Fund Report.

This is not a demand problem. It’s an infrastructure problem. And it’s exactly what Binance Capital Connect was built to address.

The Problem Is Older Than Crypto: Top Managers Get 80% of Capital

Capital raising in traditional finance is already relationship-driven and top-heavy. Over 85% of institutional investors source new manager relationships through personal networks or prime broker capital introduction desks, per AIMA research on emerging manager capital raising. The top 20% of managers are responsible for about 80% of capital deployment, per AIMA's Private Credit Investor Forum findings.

The irony: emerging managers with sub-$500 million AUM delivered 16.23% annualized returns over 2020 to 2025, compared to 8.53% for larger players, according to IG Prime. They outperform, but they can’t raise. The system rewards size over signal.

In crypto, the gap is even wider. There is no prime broker capital introduction equivalent. No standardized performance data or benchmarking framework. 47% of crypto fund managers confirmed rising investor demand in 2025, but distribution channels haven’t kept pace, per AIMA. Many rely on Telegram, personal networks, and conferences to find capital.

Three Gaps That Need Closing

Discovery

Over 85% of institutional investors source new managers through personal networks or prime brokers, per AIMA. In crypto, there is no equivalent. Investors have no centralized marketplace to browse, compare, and evaluate strategies on standardized metrics.

Diligence

There is no standardized performance data or benchmarking framework across crypto fund managers. Investors can’t compare NAV, Sharpe ratio, maximum drawdown, or gross vs net returns on equal footing.

Distribution

Emerging managers outperform larger ones by nearly 2x, per IG Prime, yet they can’t raise capital. In crypto, no institutional channel exists for independent trading teams to reach verified investors.

The Marketplace That Closes All Three: Capital Connect

Capital Connect is an open, exchange-native strategy marketplace on Binance that connects verified and eligible institutional investors with independent trading teams. It covers active strategies across digital and traditional assets, with full performance transparency and zero platform fee.

Investors browse multiple trading teams and strategy types in one place, with Binance-verified performance data displayed side by side: NAV, Sharpe ratio, Sortino ratio, max drawdown, and gross vs net returns. No Telegram groups, no conference matchmaking, no third-party platforms to navigate. 

When the market changes, investors can switch strategies on the same platform. For trading teams, Capital Connect provides access to a verified institutional investor base already embedded in the Binance ecosystem.

Getting Started with Capital Connect

For Trading Teams

  1. Complete Binance KYB verification

  2. Contact your dedicated Account Manager to apply for access to Capital Connect with license proof

  3. Binance Compliance and Ops review all applications before activation

For Investors

Capital Connect is available to KYC or KYB-verified Binance users who meet one of the following criteria: VIP Level 3 or above, total assets on Binance of $1,000,000 USD equivalent or above, or external asset proof of $1,000,000 USD submitted for review.

How it works:

  1. Browse: Explore active strategies across digital and traditional assets from a curated selection of independent trading teams, with full performance data

  2. Evaluate: Compare NAV, Sharpe ratio, max drawdown, and gross vs net returns

  3. Invest: Allocate with zero platform fee

  4. Monitor and switch: Track verified performance data across your allocated strategies, and switch or adjust your allocations as market conditions evolve. All on Binance.

Final Thoughts

The institutional wave into digital assets isn’t slowing down. It’s accelerating. But without infrastructure for active strategy allocation, capital will continue to flow into passive products by default, and the managers best positioned to generate alpha will continue to struggle for capital.

The managers who outperform shouldn’t be the ones struggling to raise. Closing that gap takes more than another fund or partnership. It takes a marketplace built to make performance visible and capital movable. Performance should be the thing that raises capital, not proximity to it. Capital Connect makes that possible.

The Blockchain 100 Awards Return in 2026 to Recognize Leading Finance Creators

2026-10-13

Main Takeaways

  • The Blockchain 100 returns for its second edition in 2026, combining annual awards with a year-round video interview series highlighting creators across the financial industry.

  • Launched in 2025, the inaugural awards recognized 100 creators across seven categories, culminating in a ceremony during Binance Blockchain Week in Dubai.

  • The 2026 edition expands recognition to creators across crypto and traditional finance, with public nominations opening October 13 and the awards ceremony taking place on November 29 during Binance Blockchain Week in Bangkok.

Content creators play an important role in the crypto industry, helping audiences understand emerging technologies, navigate financial markets, and make informed decisions. At Binance, we believe that creators who dedicate their time and expertise to educating their communities deserve recognition.

That belief led to the launch of The Blockchain 100 in 2025, an initiative that combines annual awards with a year-round video interview series. The awards recognize creators for their contributions to the industry, while the interviews explore the careers and perspectives of leading voices in crypto.

Now in its second year, The Blockchain 100 returns with an expanded focus on creators across crypto and traditional finance. Public nominations open on October 13, giving you an opportunity to support your favorite creators ahead of the awards ceremony at Binance Blockchain Week 2026 in Bangkok on November 29.

Why Binance Created The Blockchain 100

The Blockchain 100 was established to recognize creators who contribute to public understanding of blockchain technology, digital assets, and financial markets, from established industry voices to emerging creators working across different areas of crypto and financial education.

That work takes many forms. Independent researchers analyze blockchain developments, educators introduce newcomers to crypto fundamentals, and community leaders facilitate discussions and share knowledge with their audiences.

Community participation is a central part of The Blockchain 100. Through nominations and voting, audiences help identify creators whose work they value, giving the wider community a role in determining who receives recognition.

The awards also provide opportunities for creators to connect with new audiences through Binance's global community, industry partners, and dedicated content initiatives.

Looking Back at The Blockchain 100 in 2025

The inaugural edition of The Blockchain 100 Awards launched in 2025, inviting the global crypto community to nominate creators who had contributed to blockchain education and industry development.

Following public nominations and community voting, 100 creators were recognized across seven categories: Industry Advocate, Independent Researcher, Trader, Community Builder, Video and Live Creator, Crypto Press, and Rising Star.

The first edition concluded with an awards ceremony on December 3, 2025, during Binance Blockchain Week in Dubai. The event brought together creators from across the industry to celebrate their achievements and connect with fellow community members.

Beyond the Awards: The Blockchain 100 Video Series

The Blockchain 100 extends beyond the annual awards ceremony through a year-round video interview series featuring voices from across the crypto industry. The interviews give guests an opportunity to discuss their work, share personal experiences, and address developments shaping the space.

The series has featured Arthur Hayes, Benjamin Cowen, Wendy O, Eleanor Terrett, and Silvio Micali, among others. Bringing together individuals with backgrounds in trading, research, journalism, and blockchain technology, the interviews offer perspectives from different areas of the industry.

By exploring the professional journeys and experiences of its guests, the series adds a personal dimension to The Blockchain 100. It gives audiences a better understanding of the people behind the research, commentary, and educational content they encounter.

What’s New for The Blockchain 100 in 2026

Building on its inaugural edition, The Blockchain 100 returns in 2026 with an expanded scope that includes creators from both cryptocurrency and traditional finance.

This reflects the fact that financial education spans more than blockchain technology and digital assets. It also includes traditional markets and economic developments. Including creators from traditional finance allows The Blockchain 100 to recognize a broader mix of expertise and perspectives.

The 2026 awards will continue to recognize creators working across different content formats and areas of specialization, from market analysis and research to educational videos and community discussions.

How to Participate in The Blockchain 100 Awards 2026

The Blockchain 100 invites the community to help recognize creators whose work has contributed to financial education across crypto and traditional finance. Whether you follow their market analysis, educational content, or industry commentary, you can support the voices you value through public nominations and voting.

Public nominations are open October 13–16, allowing community members to put forward eligible creators for consideration. Creators can also nominate themselves.

Community voting takes place on Binance Square from October 19 to 28. Verified Binance users who have completed Know Your Customer (KYC) verification can cast one vote per award track each day, giving them an opportunity to support their preferred nominees throughout the voting period.

Winners will be announced on October 29, ahead of the awards ceremony on November 29 during Binance Blockchain Week 2026.

Final Thoughts

With its second edition approaching, The Blockchain 100 continues to recognize the creators helping audiences better understand crypto and financial markets. The expansion into traditional finance brings additional voices into the awards, while the video interview series continues to share their experiences throughout the year.

We invite the community to take part in recognizing creators whose work they value. Visit the official awards page to learn more about The Blockchain 100 and participate in nominations and voting.

Binance OTC & Execution Services Insights – October 2026

2026-10-12

Main Takeaways

  • Despite the Fed's first rate hike since 2023 and the CLARITY Act's 49-50 Senate defeat, institutional flows did not flinch.

  • ETF inflows returned strongly in the week of September 21, helping BTC break out of its $75,000-$82,000 range and hit a local high near $87,500.

  • The OTC desk saw near-complete altcoin rotation from August, sustained off-ramp activity across MENA and LATAM, and settled 5 million BFUSD across two trades in under 10 minutes.

In this ninth edition of the Binance OTC & Execution Services monthly digest, we recap a September where flows outpaced a hawkish turn in policy.

The Fed delivered its first hike since 2023, and the CLARITY Act's 49-50 Senate defeat likely pushed U.S. market-structure legislation to 2027. Yet ETF demand returned, with around $1.5 billion into BTC and $412 million into ETH in the week of September 21. BTC also broke out of its $75,000-$82,000 range, and sentiment held in greed all month.

We will also cover what client flows on the Binance OTC desk reveal about institutional positioning: a near-complete rotation in altcoin demand, continued off-ramping across MENA and LATAM, and a 5 million BFUSD-to-USDT redemption completed in about 10 minutes instead of the standard 2 days.

What’s New at Binance OTC & Execution Services

Based on client feedback, we have made Binance OTC & Execution Services easier to access. The desk is now reachable directly from the Institutional tab at the top of the Binance homepage. We are also expanding the suite to include bStocks. More details coming soon.

September 2026 Crypto Market Analysis: Flows Outpace a Hawkish Turn

Macro and Policy: The Fed Turns Hawkish

On September 16, the Fed delivered the hike that August's minutes had signaled: a unanimous 0.25 percentage point increase from 3.75% to 4.00%, its first since 2023, with another projected before year-end. The BOJ and ECB are also tightening, which puts pressure on global liquidity. 

With USD/JPY near 160, a sharp yen rally that forces carry trades to unwind is still the main tail risk. Treasury buybacks began on September 9, but the 10-year yield still rose to about 4.96%. The desk now sees buybacks as a way to keep the bond market running smoothly, not as new liquidity.

In Washington, the CLARITY Act failed a 49-50 Senate vote on September 15, likely delaying U.S. crypto market-structure legislation until 2027. Coinbase and Circle fell 8-10%, while BTC and ETH dipped far less. Stablecoins — already covered by the GENIUS Act — barely moved.

Sentiment and Flows: From Selective to Risk-On

ETF demand was uneven early in the month, as an inflow of about $723 million on September 3 soon turned into outflows. It came back strongly in the week of September 21, with about $1.5 billion into BTC ETFs and about $412 million into ETH ETFs, the strongest week since mid-August. The Fear and Greed Index stayed in greed all month and read 73 in late September.

Market Structure and BTC Outlook

BTC spent three weeks in a tight $75,000-$82,000 range while holding above the downtrend line from its $126,199 high, a sign of base-building rather than further decline. 

After the Fed meeting, it broke higher, hitting a local high near $87,500 before settling at about $84,200. ETF buying drove the move, and short covering sped it up. However, longs now carry more leverage than shorts, which leaves the market exposed if momentum stalls.

The desk is tactically constructive but cautious on macro. The next targets are $85,000-$89,000, then $93,000. A decisive close below $74,000 would bring $68,000-$71,000 back into view.

Observations on the Binance OTC Desk 

Crypto trading activity on the Binance OTC desk rose across both majors and altcoins in September. Compared with August, the altcoins traded almost completely changed, and only LRC and POL carried over. POL/USDT was our top crypto/stablecoin pair.

In September we traded:

Majors: BNB, BTC, DOGE, ETH, SOL, TRX

Stables: KGST, RWUSD, USDC, USDS, USDT, XUSD

Alts: AR, ASTER, DOT, HBAR, INJ, LRC, PEPE, PENGU, PONS, POL, PUMP, RDNT, STX, VANRY, WBTC, ZEN

“I Think We’re in a Gold Rush” – Michael Saylor on Bitcoin, Where We Stand, and its Future

2026-10-09

Main Takeaways

  • In late September, Binance’s Jessica Walker sat down with Michael Saylor – Founder and Executive Chairman of Strategy Inc., and arguably Bitcoin’s largest proponent – for a wide-ranging interview on our YouTube channel.

  • Topics included the metrics Saylor watches for in the market, his core thesis that Bitcoin is emerging as “Digital Capital”, and the notion that we’re currently in a digital asset “gold rush” from now through 2035.

  • Read on to hear Michael Saylor give his hot takes on Bitcoin and where the crypto economy is heading.

Whether you dabble in crypto or follow the market religiously, you’ve probably heard of  Michael Saylor, one of the most recognizable voices in Bitcoin and the mind behind Strategy’s long-running BTC accumulation strategy. 

Saylor has helped shape the mainstream conversation around Bitcoin as a balance-sheet asset, and his views are closely watched across crypto and traditional finance.

In a wide-ranging interview with Binance’s Jessica Walker on our YouTube channel, Saylor unpacked his latest takes on Bitcoin, from the market signals he watches to his view of Bitcoin as “Digital Capital.” He also explained why he frames the years through 2035 as a digital asset “gold rush,” and how Strategy’s BTC accumulation and digital credit ambitions connect to that timeline. 

Watch the Full Interview →

What Saylor Watches in the Market

“We normally look at the 200-week moving average, and we look at the premium or the discount to that 200-week moving average.”

For Saylor, the 200-week moving average is one of his core reference points, specifically when the market resets and looks for footing. He also touched on recent market behavior. In his view, capital rotated into the AI sector and major private-market fundraising rounds, pulling liquidity away from crypto in the short term.

Bitcoin as “Digital Capital” and Four Key Drivers for Adoption

Saylor’s core thesis is that Bitcoin is emerging as “Digital Capital,” a long-term store of value that can be held globally and used as a foundation for other financial products. He described four drivers that can expand adoption over time:

  • Securitization: ETFs and wrapped Bitcoin products that make BTC exposure easier to hold in traditional wrappers.

  • Treasury companies: public companies building equity structures on top of Bitcoin holdings.

  • Digital Credit: instruments designed to offer a different volatility and cash-flow profile than holding BTC directly.

  • Bank credit: banks custodying BTC and extending credit against it.

Drawing an analogy to other asset classes, Saylor argues that credit availability can influence how widely an asset is held and financed. This is his view of how adoption could evolve across traditional financial infrastructure.

Strategy’s Approach to Accumulating BTC

Strategy’s BTC purchases have been closely watched for years, and they’re often treated as a signal for how public companies might approach Bitcoin on a balance sheet. People often wonder: is there a target, or a point where the buying stops? We can put that question to rest because, according to Saylor, there is no target in mind.

“We don’t have any particular target. We accumulate Bitcoin as we raise capital.”

Why Strategy Built Digital Credit

A key part of the conversation was Saylor’s explanation for why buying Bitcoin directly isn’t suitable for all investors. Many portfolios struggle to absorb BTC’s volatility, even if the investor strongly believes in the long-term thesis. “Digital Credit” such as STRC, in his framing, exists to repackage Bitcoin exposure into instruments that offer a different volatility and cash-flow profile. 

To make the point concrete, Saylor illustrated two analogies:

  1. Crude oil versus gasoline: the raw energy is there, but many “engines” need crude oil refined into a form they can use.

  2. A fighter jet versus a passenger jet: BTC is a high-performance vehicle, while Digital Credit is built for smoother travel.

“And the way we describe it is Bitcoin is like a fighter jet, and Digital Credit like STRC is like a passenger jet.”

STRC vs. Gold, and Strategy’s Bitcoin

When asked how STRC differs from gold and tokenized gold, Saylor separated capital from credit. Gold and Bitcoin are forms of capital, while STRC is credit built on top of “Digital Capital,” drawing comparisons to historical gold-backed credit instruments.

STRC, also known as “Stretch,” is a Nasdaq-listed perpetual preferred stock issued by Strategy that pays a cash dividend. Strategy actively manages STRC around its $100 par value, with the ability to issue shares above $100 and repurchase shares below $100. At the time of recording, Strategy’s balance sheet was worth over 840,000 bitcoin.

“We own more than 4% of all the Bitcoin that will ever exist.”

Disclaimer: BTC holdings, market figures, yields, and product terms may change. Bitcoin and securities such as STRC carry different risks; neither future returns nor dividends are guaranteed. Review current disclosures before making an investment decision. 

Are We Still Early? Saylor’s “Gold Rush” Thesis

“I think the crypto economy is maybe $3 trillion right now… All the other assets in the economy are $1,000 trillion or $1,200 trillion.”

Toward the end of the interview, Saylor answered the one question every crypto investor has on their mind: where is bitcoin on the adoption curve. In other words, are we still early? 

“I think we’re in a gold rush between now and the year 2035.”

Relative to broader global asset markets, Saylor argues that the crypto economy is small and remains in a phase that he describes as “hyper-growth mode”. He also anchored his “early” view to supply dynamics. By 2035, Saylor believes 99% of all bitcoin will have been mined, describing the period between now and 2035 as a “gold rush” for digital assets.

AI Abundance and “Trophy Assets”

Amid all the talk about Bitcoin and digital assets, the conversation also touched on AI, robotics, and what Saylor thinks gets cheaper versus what stays scarce. His view is that technology drives down the cost of things that can be produced at scale, while certain “trophy assets” remain scarce by definition.

“The robots can’t create more beachfront real estate in Palm Beach.”

Pointing to examples like mountains and art, Saylor argued that robots can’t produce another Picasso, nor can they manufacture more coastline. Scarce desirable assets stay scarce, even if technology makes more services and everyday goods – food, water, lawyers, etc. –  cheaper.

TL;DR

  • Saylor watches Bitcoin’s 200-week moving average and institutional capital flows to frame market structure.

  • He describes Bitcoin as “digital capital,” with adoption expanding through ETFs, treasury companies, digital credit, and bank credit.

  • Strategy’s BTC accumulation has no fixed target, only that it scales with capital raising.

  • STRC is positioned as “digital credit,” built for investors who want a different volatility and cash-flow profile than holding BTC directly.

  • Saylor frames 2026–2035 as a key window for adoption, calling it a digital asset “gold rush.”

Tokenized equities are distributed across multiple chains, but in 2026, BNB Chain has become a key venue. This is where the “on-chain” part becomes tangible. Once an asset can be transferred, collateralized, and deployed across protocols, it starts to behave like a composable building block rather than a static position.

Final Thoughts

Tokenized equities passed $3B in 2026, but the more important signal is how they’re being used. Holder counts are rising, transfer activity has grown, and DeFi usage is climbing — all signs of real adoption, not just capital inflow. The result looks less like a separate crypto universe and more like a broader financial network, where different asset types can be held, moved, and used side by side. Within this shift, bStocks gives users tokenized security exposure on crypto rails, including the capability to trade 24/7 and move between the exchange and self-custody, on their own terms.

How Binance Keeps Your Crypto Safe: Key Security Numbers, Scam Alerts, and the SAFU Fund

2026-10-07

Main Takeaways

  • In the first half of 2026, Binance’s AI-assisted risk systems helped protect more than 8 million users and prevent approximately $4.6 billion in potential losses.

  • Eight layers of account protection form a single, real-time response — alerting, verifying, and intervening in proportion to the risk, so your experience stays smooth and your account stays secure.

  • Behind these systems is the Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU), an emergency reserve worth $1 billion, backed by free security education that helps users do their part too.

At Binance, security doesn't depend on one tool. It works in layers: systems that stop threats in real time, account-level protections that respond in proportion to risk, education that helps users protect themselves, and an emergency fund for the worst cases. Here's how each layer performed in the first half of 2026, and what it means for keeping your crypto safe.

How Binance’s AI Stopped $4.6 Billion in Losses

Binance's AI-assisted risk systems check activity in real time and flag threats before they reach users, powered by more than 100 AI models working across anti-fraud and anti-scam controls. In H1 2026, these systems intercepted millions of scam and phishing attempts, blacklisted more than 42,000 malicious addresses, and issued over 14,000 real-time warnings every day. 

These models now make 80% to 90% of real-time risk decisions, with human reviewers stepping in on the cases that need closer judgment. Together, these measures protected more than 8 million users and prevented approximately $4.6 billion in potential losses.

Binance’s 8-Level Account Protection

On Binance, account protection is a layered system built on a real-time risk detection engine, designed to keep the crypto experience smooth and secure across our platform.

1. Multi-channel notifications: When suspicious activity is detected, Binance alerts you via email and in-app messages.

2. OTP verification: Sensitive actions require a unique, time-sensitive one-time password, so login details alone aren't enough for an attacker to proceed.

3. Roaming verification: Logins or actions from a new device, location, or unusual IP address triggers additional verification.

4. Passkey authentication (FIDO): Binance supports passkeys, a device-bound cryptographic login method (via Face ID/Touch ID) that is highly resistant to phishing and password theft.

5. Facial recognition: For higher-risk actions, facial recognition is required.

6. Forced logouts: If account takeover is suspected, Binance can force a hard reset, logging out all active sessions across devices so you can reset your password and secure the account.

7. Single withdrawal rejection: A suspicious withdrawal can be blocked individually. You're notified, and can retry after additional verification if it was you.

8. Withdrawal function block: At the highest risk level, withdrawals may be temporarily paused as a final safeguard. Withdrawals resume only after security checks and confirmation from the account owner.

Emergency Reserves: $1 Billion in the SAFU Fund

The Secure Asset Fund for Users (SAFU) is an emergency reserve that Binance set up in July 2018. SAFU funds protect user assets in extreme cases, such as security breaches or platform-level incidents. As of 2026, the fund holds approximately $1 billion.

SAFU is a safety net for when other protections fall short, kept separate from operational accounts. If a security incident causes users to lose funds, Binance may use SAFU assets to compensate affected users.

Scam Education: Strengthening the Last Line of Defense

Our systems can stop millions of threats, and SAFU funds are in place for extreme cases. But no system can make every decision for you. You decide whether to click a link, share a verification code, or approve a transaction. That makes you the last line of defense. That’s why we focus on giving you the knowledge to make that call with confidence.

Scams change quickly, so our security blog series breaks down emerging scam tactics as they appear, with 10 deep dives published since the start of 2026. There’s also a consolidated guide, which puts the key lessons in one place. If you’d like a more structured approach, our free Binance Academy course on managing risk teaches you how to protect yourself. Pick whichever works for you, the outcome is the same: knowing what to watch for.

Final Thoughts

Real-time AI detection, account protection, ongoing education, and the SAFU fund all work together to keep users safe. The numbers from H1 2026 show that these layers work, but security is also a shared effort. Staying informed through our security series and Binance Academy courses, and keeping your account’s security settings up to date, are two of the simplest ways to protect your assets. The systems are watching. Make sure you are too.

Main Takeaways

  • On October 5, we unveiled Binance Intelligence – our most ambitious set of products designed to put institutional-grade artificial intelligence in every trader’s hands.

  • Binance Intelligence covers three products: Agent OS for developers looking to build agents, Binance AI for everyday app users, and Binance AI Pro for advanced users who want to deploy automated trading workflows.

  • Binance AI is free and launches today for eligible users in New Zealand, with global rollout over the coming days. AI Pro will launch in the coming weeks.

Today, we unveiled Binance Intelligence, a new AI layer built directly into the Binance experience. In a special livestream, Co-CEO Richard Teng and VP of Product Jeff Li presented three products that reimagine how finance works, and how it works for our users: 1) Agent OS, 2) Binance AI, and 3) Binance AI Pro. 

"Finance shouldn't ask you to become an expert first. It should meet you where you are. With Binance Intelligence, it does." - Richard Teng

Closing the Gap with AI

The core philosophy behind Binance Intelligence starts at the root problem for many users. So much financial information – stocks, commodities, crypto, perpetuals, yield, just to name a few – is now accessible to millions globally. Binance Intelligence gives users the tools to interpret that information and act on it. 

From years of building with AI, including over 100 models across our compliance and risk systems, Binance Intelligence takes everything we've learned and puts it directly into the products our users rely on.

Now, when you open the app, you’ll have the technology that once only belonged to hedge funds and financial experts, working around the clock to help you make better informed decisions.

Agent OS: Build AI Agents With Binance Capabilities

In August, we launched Agent OS, giving our more tech-savvy customers a dedicated toolkit to equip their AI agents with Binance capabilities, including trading, access to market data, and more. 

Not only does Agent OS make building powerful agents a more seamless experience, it also comes with advanced safety controls, including mandatory sub-accounts for agents, prohibited agent withdrawals, and granular permissions. Developers can revoke access at any time, including an emergency stop function that disconnects all agents.

In the first month alone, we’ve seen a variety of agent use cases, from trading bots and research assistants to full-on automated hedging strategies.

Binance AI: A Free 24/7 Personal Assistant

Designed for all levels of experience, Binance AI is a 24/7 personal assistant that pays attention to what matters most to you. Where enabled, Binance AI can personalize your experience based on information such as your product usage, preferences and holdings. Every user will see a different dashboard when they open the app.

Personalized Features

  • Smart Tool Tips: When you open a product you haven’t used before, a tip shows you how it works, then disappears once you’ve got the hang of it.

  • Market Brief: An AI summary covering crypto, stocks, and macro updates throughout the day; you can read it or listen to it like a mini-podcast.

  • Smart Alert: Stay on top of the market even when you’re away from the screen. Get a real-time voice call when your price targets or signal triggers hit.

  • PnL Recap and Smart Tracker: Know where your portfolio stands at a glance. A daily summary of your gains and losses, plus alerts when your favorite assets are moving.

More AI-Powered Widgets

  • Market Buzz, Macro Insight, and Hot Sector: See trending conversations and sentiment from across the crypto community, the policy decisions and economic data behind price moves, and which crypto sectors capital is flowing into in real time.

  • Trade Ideas and Trader Picks: Find ideas for your next trade without spending hours on the charts. Trade Ideas draws on live market signals and your trading profile, and Trader Picks lets you see what moves pro and celebrity traders are making.

  • Indices and K-line integration: Read the market faster, even if technical analysis isn’t your strength. Track crypto and traditional market indices in one view, and see AI annotations on candlestick charts that mark key patterns, support and resistance levels, and trend signals.

And here’s the part you’ll love, Binance AI is completely free to use and goes live today for all eligible users in New Zealand, with global rollout to follow in the coming days. Stay tuned.

AI Pro: Build Trading Workflows With No Code

The final product presented, AI Pro, turns ideas into automated trading workflows with zero coding required. Describe what you want to build in plain language, test it against the market with paper trading, and then run it live 24/7. We’ve built an “agent and executor” directly into Binance. Beyond trading, you can also ask AI Pro to put together a daily market report or alert you when BTC hits key price levels.

“Prompt. Test. Trade. That's AI Pro.” - Jeff Li

When it comes to safety, a workflow will not be activated until you review and approve it. Once activated, it can execute within the permissions, budgets, and risk limits you have set. AI Pro only executes with funds in the sub-account you've authorized.

AI Pro will launch with a free version using credits refreshed weekly, with a paid subscription planned later. 

Final Thoughts

Over nine years, Binance has grown into one integrated platform with over 300 million users, $156 trillion in cumulative trading volume, and 43% of the world's crypto holders. Binance has opened access to crypto, then to payments, yield, and traditional markets. 

The next step is making all of that easier to understand and use, a financial evolution, where everyone can access all finance on Binance. 

"The freedom of money should belong to everyone, and with AI, we can finally put it in the hands of every single user." - Richard Teng

Binance AI is rolling out globally over the coming days, and Binance AI Pro will follow in the coming weeks. If you missed the livestream, you can watch our recording.

Binance Global Policy Insights: Know Your Agent

2026-10-01

Prepared by 

  • Binance Global Policy | October 2026

  • Steven McWhirter, Global Policy Lead

  • Diego Montes Serralde, Global Policy Manager

  • With the expert contribution of Tanveer Kalooji

Main Takeaways

  • Agentic AI could materially improve financial crime compliance. AI agents can analyse information across multiple systems, investigate alerts, identify relationships, monitor regulatory changes and prepare case assessments. Used responsibly, they could reduce low-value manual work and allow compliance professionals to focus on higher-risk cases and consequential decisions.

  • Autonomy creates a new accountability challenge. Once AI systems can use tools, delegate tasks, alter records or initiate transactions, institutions must be able to establish which agent acted, who authorised it, what mandate it held and who remains responsible for the outcome.

  • Know Your Agent (“KYA”) should complement, rather than replace, KYC. KYC establishes the identity and risk profile of the customer or legal entity. KYA establishes the identity, provenance, authority, permissions and operating constraints of the software acting on their behalf.

  • The strongest governance model separates intelligence from control. AI agents may analyse, prioritise and recommend, while consequential actions should remain subject to defined policy controls, explicit authorisation thresholds, runtime monitoring and proportionate human or institutional oversight. 

  • Policy attention is already moving in this direction. Recent work in the UK and Singapore points to the need for clearer safeguards around agent identity, delegated authority, runtime controls and machine-to-machine authentication, particularly as agentic payments become an early test case for broader autonomous financial activity.

1. Introduction

Financial crime compliance has evolved alongside the financial system it is intended to protect. As payments became faster, financial services became more digital and markets became increasingly global, compliance functions adopted automated screening, transaction-monitoring systems, blockchain analytics and machine-learning models. Agentic artificial intelligence may represent the next stage of that evolution.

Unlike a conventional rules engine, which follows predefined instructions, or a generative AI application, which produces content in response to a prompt, an AI agent can pursue an objective through a sequence of actions. It may retrieve information from multiple systems, determine which tools to use, compare alternative courses of action and adapt its workflow as circumstances change.

In an AML context, an agent could receive a transaction-monitoring alert, review the customer profile, analyse linked accounts and wallets, consult relevant typologies, prepare an investigative chronology and recommend whether the case should be escalated. Several specialised agents could divide those tasks across identity verification, sanctions screening, blockchain tracing and case management, before presenting a consolidated assessment to a human investigator.

This could materially improve the effectiveness of compliance. It could also introduce new risks.

A compliance agent may access highly sensitive information, make inferences about customers, alter risk classifications or close alerts. An agent involved in payments may go further by selecting a route, confirming that predefined conditions have been met or initiating a transaction under delegated authority. If those systems are not properly identified, permissioned and monitored, institutions may struggle to reconstruct how an outcome was reached or determine where responsibility lies. The questions around liability, oversight and control become more acute. Once software can take autonomous or semi-autonomous steps toward a goal, rather than merely generate analysis, institutions must be able to determine whether the agent acted within its mandate, whether appropriate oversight was maintained, and who remains responsible for the outcome.

The central policy question is, therefore, how institutions and regulators can preserve identity, authority and accountability when software begins to act within the compliance and payment architecture.

This paper argues that a Know Your Agent, or KYA, framework could provide an important part of the answer. KYA would not displace KYC, customer due diligence or existing AML/CFT obligations, including applicable transaction-monitoring and payment-transparency requirements. It would provide an additional control layer for software agents by establishing who or what the agent is, which person or organisation it represents, what it is permitted to do and how its conduct can be limited, verified and, where necessary, stopped.

An AI agent should not be permitted to undertake a consequential financial or compliance action unless its identity can be authenticated, its authority is defined and appropriately bounded, and its conduct can be attributed to an accountable principal.

2. What is Agentic AI?

Agentic AI refers to systems that can pursue an objective through a sequence of actions, rather than merely responding to a single instruction. An agent may determine which steps are required, retrieve information from different systems, use external tools and adjust its approach as new information becomes available.

Agentic AI is not necessarily a distinct model category. In practice, an agentic system may combine one or more AI models with tools, memory, orchestration, external data sources and permissions that enable it to pursue objectives and take actions.

These systems exist on a spectrum. Some operate as assistants that prepare recommendations for human approval, while others can perform defined tasks or initiate actions within the permissions they have been granted. The governance implications become more significant as an AI system moves from producing information to acting on it.

The World Economic Forum has described this development as requiring governance models that take into account an agent’s role, autonomy, authority, predictability and operational context. The United Kingdom’s Digital Regulation Cooperation Forum similarly characterises agentic AI as a shift from AI as a tool to AI as an actor that can assess goals, plan workflows and execute actions affecting real-world environments.

Safeguards should, therefore, depend on what a system is capable of doing in practice, rather than labels as an “AI agent.”

3. From compliance automation to agentic compliance

The financial sector already uses AI across fraud detection, AML monitoring, customer-risk assessment, sanctions screening and operational processes. Agentic AI builds on those capabilities by connecting separate analytical functions into adaptive workflows that can gather evidence, assess context and prepare actions for human or rules-based approval.

A. Customer due diligence and onboarding

An onboarding agent could collect information from approved sources, identify missing documents, compare records and flag inconsistencies. For legal entities, it might analyse corporate registries, ownership structures and beneficial ownership information. For individuals, it could support identity verification, sanctions screening and initial risk classification.

The institution would remain responsible for the adequacy of its customer due diligence. The value lies in reducing fragmented manual processes and directing human attention toward higher-risk or ambiguous cases.

B. Transaction monitoring and investigations

Traditional monitoring systems frequently generate high volumes of alerts based on static rules and thresholds. Agentic AI may support more contextual assessment by examining transactions against the customer’s profile, counterparties, previous behaviour and wider transaction network.

In crypto markets, an agent could combine account-level information with blockchain analytics to identify exposure to sanctioned or high-risk addresses, rapid movement through multiple wallets, cross-chain obfuscation or patterns associated with scams and laundering typologies. This direction is increasingly recognised in international AML/CFT policy. FATF’s 2026 work notes that advances in artificial intelligence, machine learning and big-data analytics have the potential to enhance blockchain analytics and other tools used to detect and monitor suspicious activity.

Once an alert is generated, an investigative agent could build a chronology, map the movement of funds from fiat on-ramps into digital assets, trace subsequent wallet activity across chains and counterparties, identify any off-ramp activity, retrieve supporting records, and draft a case narrative. A separate agent could test whether the proposed conclusion is supported by the evidence and identify contradictory information or unsupported assumptions.

This could improve the use of compliance resources by reducing administrative work and allowing investigators to focus on judgment-intensive cases. It could also improve auditability where the data sources, tool calls, intermediate findings and approvals are retained as part of a unified evidentiary record. Importantly, greater analytical capability does not remove the need for expert judgment. FATF’s 2026 work similarly emphasises that advanced blockchain analytics are most effective when combined with traditional investigative techniques and expert human assessment.

Where a report is being considered, a separate agent or control function could verify that the draft narrative is supported by source records and satisfies the institution’s escalation criteria.

Consequential decisions, including decisions to file a suspicious activity or transaction report, terminate a customer relationship or impose another material restriction, should remain subject to appropriate validation and accountable human or institutional oversight, consistent with applicable law and supervisory expectations. 

C. Sanctions and adverse media monitoring

Sanctions compliance increasingly requires institutions to look beyond direct name matching and assess ownership, control, indirect exposure and geographic restrictions and links to sanctioned or high-risk activity, rather than relying on direct name matching alone.

An agent could monitor list changes, identify potentially affected customers, analyse complex ownership structures and prioritise cases according to confidence and urgency.

It could support adverse-media screening by assessing whether a result is a true customer match, whether the source is credible and current, whether the allegations are relevant to the institution’s risk appetite, and whether escalation or further due diligence is warranted.

These capabilities could allow institutions to respond more quickly to emerging threats, adverse-media developments, and changing designations, but they also introduce risks if an agent relies on inaccurate sources, weak entity resolution, outdated reporting, or unsupported inferences.

D. Regulatory change and control mapping

AML obligations evolve through legislation, regulatory rules, guidance and enforcement decisions. An AI agent could monitor relevant sources, identify amendments and map them against the firm’s policies, products and controls.

This could support more continuous compliance management and help institutions identify where monitoring scenarios, risk indicators or procedures require adjustment. Legal and compliance professionals would nevertheless need to validate interpretations, particularly where requirements are ambiguous or differ across jurisdictions.

Across these use cases, the value of agentic AI lies not merely in speed. It lies in its ability to connect fragmented information, assess activity in context and allow human expertise to be focused where judgment matters most.

Those benefits are conditional. Agents may hallucinate, misinterpret information or rely on weak sources. Investigators may defer excessively to apparently sophisticated recommendations. Models trained on historical decisions may reproduce earlier biases, while agents connected to external tools may be exposed to prompt injection, data leakage or unauthorised actions.

The objective should not, therefore, be unrestricted automation, but controlled delegation: agents may support analysis, prioritisation, and recommendation, while consequential outcomes remain subject to deterministic safeguards, documented approvals and human or institutional accountability.

The same architecture could support the controlled use of information received through public-private partnerships, including emerging typologies and risk indicators. As such information becomes more structured and machine-readable, institutions will need to ensure that agents access and use it only within defined legal, confidentiality and purpose limitations.

4. Why is KYC not enough?

KYC answers a foundational question: who is the customer? In an agentic environment, that question remains essential but is no longer sufficient.

An institution may know the customer behind an account while remaining unable to determine whether a particular instruction originated from the customer, an authorised agent, a compromised agent or a sub-agent acting beyond its mandate.

Two agents accessing the same system may also present materially different risks. One may be authorised only to retrieve information. Another may be able to modify a customer’s risk classification, close an alert or initiate a transfer.

Institutions, therefore, need to be able to determine which agent performed a particular action, who developed, deployed and operated that agent, and on whose behalf it was acting. They should also understand the scope of the agent’s mandate, including which data, systems and tools it was permitted to access, whether it could merely recommend an action or had authority to initiate or execute it, and whether it could delegate tasks to other agents.

This assessment should also extend to the limits placed on that authority, including any financial, temporal or geographic restrictions, the mechanisms available to suspend or revoke the agent’s permissions, and the identity of the natural or legal person that ultimately remains accountable for its conduct.

KYA extends beyond conventional identity and access management. Traditional access controls generally determine whether a user or service account may enter a system and perform a defined function. KYA must also establish the agent’s relationship to its principal, the purpose and limits of its mandate, any authority to delegate tasks, and the accountable party responsible for the resulting conduct. This broader context becomes essential where an agent can operate across systems, act asynchronously or exercise discretion within a delegated objective.

The OpenID Foundation has noted that agents often act indistinguishably from human users, while existing authorisation models may be insufficient for asynchronous activity, cross-domain interactions, recursive delegation and agents operating for multiple users. KYA provides a framework for addressing these gaps.

5. What is Know Your Agent (KYA)? 

Know Your Agent can be understood as the process of identifying, authenticating, authorising and continuously governing an AI agent that acts within or interacts with a financial service.

KYA should not be treated as granting legal personality to software or applying conventional customer due diligence directly to a machine. The objective is operational accountability, while legal and regulatory responsibilities continue to attach to the relevant natural or legal persons. This is consistent with the broader technology-neutral approach reflected in FATF’s 2026 work, which distinguishes underlying software from the persons exercising control or performing regulated financial functions through it.

A KYA framework should establish the relationship among the different actors involved in an agent-mediated activity. This includes the agent itself, understood as the software instance performing the relevant task, and the principal, meaning the individual or legal entity on whose behalf the agent acts.

The framework should also identify the provider or deployer responsible for developing, operating, configuring or making the agent available, as well as the relying institution, such as a financial institution, VASP or payment provider, that permits the agent to access or interact with its systems. Clearly defining these roles is essential to determine the applicable permissions, responsibilities and lines of accountability.

These roles may overlap depending on how the agent is developed and used. For example, a financial institution may procure, deploy and rely on an internal AML agent itself. By contrast, a consumer-facing agent may be provided by a third-party technology company and authorised by the customer to interact with one or more financial institutions.

Regardless of the operating model, the agent should remain clearly linked to the individual or legal entity that is ultimately accountable for its actions.

In our view, a practical KYA framework could be structured around five layers.

  1. Agent identity and provenance: Each material agent should have a distinct identity linked to its provider, deployer, responsible legal entity, software or model version, and authentication credentials. This allows institutions to attribute an action to a specific authorised agent, rather than merely confirming that a valid user or service account was accessed.

  2. Link to an accountable principal: The agent should be linked to the individual or organisation on whose behalf it acts. While responsibilities may be allocated contractually among technology providers and regulated firms, the use of an agent should not dilute the regulated institution’s responsibility for meeting its AML/CFT obligations.

  3. Mandate and permissions: Each agent should operate under a clearly defined mandate specifying the actions, data and tools available to it and the purposes for which they may be used. Permissions should follow the principle of least privilege and, where personal or sensitive information is involved, incorporate appropriate purpose limitation, data minimisation and access controls. They should also distinguish between the ability to analyse or recommend and the authority to make or execute consequential decisions.

  4. Delegation and monitoring: Where agents may use sub-agents or external services, the permitted delegation chain should be defined and authenticated, with delegated authority remaining within the original mandate. Institutions should continuously monitor both the agent’s behaviour and, where it can initiate financial activity, the transactions generated through that authority. Monitoring should identify behaviour that exceeds permissions, departs from expected activity, indicates compromise or creates financial-crime risks requiring additional review.

  5. Revocation and auditability: Institutions should be able to suspend an agent, revoke or restrict its permissions and introduce additional human approval where necessary. Material actions should remain traceable to the agent, its principal, the authority in force, the tools and data used, any human intervention and the resulting outcome.

For consequential actions, KYA should support point-of-action verification. The relevant control layer should be capable of confirming that the agent’s identity and credentials remain valid, that the proposed action falls within its current mandate and that no approval, risk or revocation condition prevents execution.

In practical terms, a minimum KYA record would allow an institution to verify the agent’s identity, the principal it represents, the party responsible for deploying it, the scope and duration of its authority, any right to delegate, its current status and the context in which it is authorised to operate. The record should support attribution and control without implying that the agent itself assumes the regulatory status or obligations of the person on whose behalf it acts. That information should accompany the agent throughout the relevant interaction and remain available for subsequent review.

As agent-mediated activity scales, elements of the KYA record should be capable of being expressed in machine-readable and, where appropriate, cryptographically verifiable form. This could allow an agent’s identity, principal, mandate, limits, delegation rights and status to be checked consistently across financial institutions and payment infrastructures.

This type of minimum record could also support emerging trust frameworks for agentic payments, where regulators and industry are beginning to consider standardised approaches to agent identity, verification and machine-to-machine authentication.

Taken together, these five layers provide the foundation for treating AI agents as identifiable, authorised and governable participants within a financial institution’s control environment. Their practical value, however, depends on how they are embedded into day-to-day compliance processes. An AML workflow provides a useful illustration of how KYA can translate these principles into operational controls, from verifying an agent’s authority at the outset to preserving human accountability for consequential decisions.

6. KYA in practice: a controlled AML workflow

In practice, an agentic AML workflow could involve specialised agents reviewing customer information, transaction behaviour, blockchain activity and sanctions exposure. Before accessing a case, each agent’s identity, mandate and permissions would be verified. Their findings could then be consolidated and independently challenged before any recommendation is accepted.

Consequential outcomes should remain subject to fixed, rules-based controls that the agent cannot override, together with appropriate human approval. The process should preserve a record of the evidence considered, its relevant provenance and permitted use, the agents and models involved, material tool calls, any human intervention and the final decision. This reflects a clear separation of functions in which agents analyse and recommend, controls enforce mandatory requirements, and accountable humans decide where the consequences are significant.

This direction is already beginning to emerge in policy and industry practice. In July 2026, the Monetary Authority of Singapore announced the Safeguards for Agentic Finance at Runtime (“SAFR”) framework, developed with industry participants under its BuildFin.ai initiative. SAFR focuses on the need for real-time safeguards where AI agents operate in financial services, including policy-bound execution, validation before action, auditability and interoperability. Its emphasis on verifying and recording an agent’s proposed actions before execution is closely aligned with the KYA approach proposed in this paper in which agents may support financial workflows, but their actions should remain bounded by identity, authority, mandate and control requirements that can be reviewed after the fact.

7. Agentic payments and the case for KYA

The need for KYA becomes more immediate where agents can transact. The IMF has described agent-mediated payments as a potential transition from “click-to-pay” toward “decide-to-pay,” in which software agents may compare options, determine whether conditions have been met and initiate financial actions under delegated authority.

This concern is increasingly reflected in central-bank thinking. In June 2026, Sarah Breeden of the Bank of England observed that agentic AI could move payments and commerce from recommendation mode, where humans still execute transactions, toward systems in which agents automate the final step. She highlighted that this raises practical questions around how users securely provide consent and authorisation to agents, how disputes and liability should be handled for erroneous or fraudulent transactions, and how authorities can avoid fragmentation as AI firms, merchants and payment systems develop their own agent-interaction protocols.

The United Kingdom’s Financial Services AI Adoption Plan points in the same direction. It identifies agentic payments as a near-term use case for autonomous financial systems and notes that these models raise uncertainty around legal accountability, liability, consent and fraud in automated payment flows. Importantly, the Plan recommends the development of a trust framework for agentic payments built around legal and liability standards, Know Your Agent protocols, and interoperable machine-to-machine authentication. This provides a useful policy signal in which KYA is not merely an internal compliance concept, but part of the broader trust infrastructure likely to be needed as agents begin to initiate or support financial transactions.

These developments create an architectural tension. AI systems are probabilistic and adaptive, while payment infrastructures depend on predictability, legal certainty and deterministic execution.

A useful model is to separate the process into three layers. 

In crypto markets, programmable wallets and smart contracts may allow permissions to be expressed directly through code. A wallet could limit an agent to specified assets, approved addresses, transaction values or time periods, while requiring human approval where risk indicators or thresholds are triggered.

Before processing an agent-initiated transaction, a VASP or payment provider should be able to verify the identity and status of the agent, the principal it represents, the scope of its delegated authority and whether the transaction falls within that mandate. Existing transaction-level obligations and risk controls should continue to apply irrespective of whether an instruction originates from a person or an authorised agent. Depending on the activity, these may include sanctions screening, Travel Rule requirements, wallet-risk assessment and enhanced controls for higher-risk cross-chain or DeFi exposure. 

A proportionate framework should distinguish among agents that retrieve information, recommend transactions and control or transfer value. The greater the authority and potential consequence, the stronger the identity, monitoring and approval requirements should be.

This is best understood as “bounded autonomy” in which agents may operate within clearly authorised objectives, permissions and limits, but stronger safeguards should apply as their ability to affect customers, compliance outcomes or the movement of value increases.

8. Conclusion

Agentic AI could significantly strengthen financial crime compliance. It can connect fragmented information, identify relationships across large datasets, accelerate investigations and help institutions respond more dynamically to changing risks.

The same capabilities change the control environment. Once software can select tools, delegate tasks, alter records or initiate payments, institutions need to know more than who the customer is. They must know which agent acted, who it represented, what authority it held and whether its conduct remained within that authority.

Know Your Agent offers a practical framework for answering those questions. KYA is an accountability layer for software operating within the financial system.

The future AML architecture may, therefore, be understood through three complementary lenses: (1) Know Your Customer, which establishes the identity and risk profile of an individual or legal entity; (2) Know Your Transaction, which examines how value moves, why the activity is occurring and whether it is consistent with expected behaviour; and (3) Know Your Agent, which identifies the software actor involved, the authority under which it operates, the limits of its permissions and the person or entity that remains accountable for its actions.

Together, these disciplines could provide the trust architecture required for an increasingly automated financial system. As AI agents gain greater authority to influence decisions and move value, governance should follow that authority. Greater autonomy, access and potential consequence should be matched by stronger requirements for verifiable identity, bounded permissions, auditable conduct, revocation and continuing human or institutional accountability.
